extracted.intended_audience: architects, artists, handicraftsmen, students and critics of architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and prescribing principles for architectural design focused on ornamentation, material honesty, structural truth, and the moral/aesthetic duties of the architect and craftsman. Emphasizes when ornament and new materials are appropriate or become deceitful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament proportioned to distance and to the work
rubrics_metrics.description: 'a very noble proportioning of the work to the distance, the niches and statues ... being alike colossal and simple; visibly so from below, so as to induce no deception, and yet honestly and well finished above'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornament should read correctly at the viewing distance: large, simple, and honest in massing when seen from afar while still finished above. Avoid detail that deceives the eye at normal vantage points. Example: niches and statues should be colossal and simple when placed high so they remain sensible rather than deceptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delicacy at the base and greater effective quantity above
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the ornaments ... are most delicate at the base, they are often in greater effective quantity on the upper parts'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the principle that solidity in foundation is necessary while upper parts may be lighter and more pierced; use delicate bas-relief at lower levels and richer, more intricate traceries higher up to suit visual effect and structural logic. Example: Giotto's campanile combines delicate bas-reliefs at base with open tracery above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid work too good for its material or too fine to bear exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: 'work may be wasted by being too good for its material, or too fine to bear exposure'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not produce ornament so delicate or refined that it is inappropriate to the material or climate (e.g., ivory-like carving on exposed building surfaces). Such work causes anxiety and is a mismatch between finish and durability. Anti-pattern: elaborate incrustation that could not withstand a 'drifting shower or gnawing frost'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament must 'do its duty' — have distant/decorative power
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If the ornament does its duty — if it is ornament, and its points of shade and light tell in the general effect, we shall not be offended...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ornament by its contribution to the overall effect (shade, light, massing) rather than by microscopic ingenuity. Ornament that only works up close and fails to contribute to the general decorative power is meaningless ornamentation (a mere incrustation). Scoring note: valuable ornament speaks even 'to the uninquiring eye' and increases mystery and majesty rather than diminishes them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Luxuriance is permissible when ornament is good; 'overcharged' only when bad
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Ornament cannot be overcharged if it be good, and is always overcharged when it is bad.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not condemn richness of ornament per se; evaluate whether each element has purpose and contributes positively. The test of 'overcharge' is whether the ornament is good and purposeful rather than merely profuse. Example: the Rouen gate — extremely numerous niches but none useless — is praised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain contrast and rests in design
rubrics_metrics.description: Styles of simplicity owe part of their pleasurableness to contrast; simple styles serve as 'rests and monotones' for ornamented work
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value both highly ornamented and simple treatments; judge a work on its role within aesthetic contrasts. Overuse of either simplicity or ornament leads to weariness; effective architecture balances them for higher effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth in architecture: avoid falsity about materials or labour
rubrics_metrics.description: 'a direct falsity of assertion respecting the nature of material, or the quantity of labor, ... is, in the full sense of the word, wrong'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess honesty: architects must not pretend materials, construction methods, or amounts of labor they did not employ. Such deceit is a moral failing of the art and a key cause of architectural degradation. Anti-patterns: painted marbling that claims to be stone; claiming carved stone where machine-cast ornament is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural Deceits — three heads (defined)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Architectural Deceits are broadly to be considered under three heads: 1st. The suggestion of a mode of structure or support, other than the true one; 2d. The painting of surfaces to represent some other material than that of which they actually consist; 3d. The use of cast or machine-made ornaments of any kind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite classification as an evaluation checklist. Each head should be examined for presence, degree, and whether customary exceptions have removed the 'deceit' quality. Examples and nuance follow in other rubrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural deceit: false suggestion of support or structure
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The suggestion of a mode of structure or support, other than the true one'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deem unacceptable deliberate suggestion that a member performs a structural role it does not (e.g., pendants implying different support). Distinguish permissible concealment (where informed observers could discern true construction) from deliberate misrepresentation (e.g., wooden shell whitewashed to look stone). When the true conditions of weight are understood, truth requires that means of support also be comprehensible. Anti-patterns: artificial suspensions or 'inadequate supports' that are affectation (condemned example: King's College Chapel piers; stunt-like suspensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment versus deception — concealment allowable within limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The architect 'is not bound to exhibit structure; ... the building will generally be the noblest which to an intelligent eye discovers the great secrets of its structure'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concealment of structure is acceptable if an intelligent observer could infer the true construction and is not actively misled. There's no dishonesty in producing impressions that differ from physical truth if the conditions of the real structure remain knowable; but once weight/support conditions are understood, concealment that contradicts them becomes dishonest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deceptive assumptions of structure — decorative members pretending duty
rubrics_metrics.description: 'deceptive assumptions of it — the introduction of members which should have, or profess to have, a duty, and have none'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag as bad practice members that mimic structural purpose without performing it (decorative buttresses, pinnacles with no work). Example: late-Gothic flying buttresses used where they are unnecessary or in forms incapable of resisting thrust; St. Ouen lantern at Rouen described as a 'basest piece of Gothic' because buttresses/pinnacles are mere show. Such mock-structure is a corruption to be guarded against.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface deceit: painting or finishing to represent other materials
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the painting of surfaces to represent some other material than that of which they actually consist (as in the marbling of wood), or the deceptive representation of sculptured ornament upon them'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider painted imitations of other materials as deceitful in architecture (though some long-used practices may have become acceptable in degree). Evaluate whether the observer is led to false belief about materiality. Example: marbling wood to look like stone is condemnable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical/cast ornament: use of machine-made ornaments is suspect
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the use of cast or machine-made ornaments of any kind'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the use of cast or machine-made ornament as a potential deceit and a diminishment of craft honesty. However, recognize that frequent usage can blunt the sense of deceit in some cases (assess degree and context). Anti-pattern: mass-produced ornament that pretends to be hand-carved or integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common exceptions exist — frequency can neutralize deceit (gilding example)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'there are certain degrees of them, which, owing to their frequent usage, or to other causes, have so far lost the nature of deceit as to be admissible; as, for instance, gilding ... is in architecture no deceit, because it is therein not understood for gold'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating suspected deceit, account for conventional meanings and reader/viewer expectations. If a treatment is not commonly understood to represent something other than itself (e.g., gilding not read as gold in architecture), it may be admissible. Use convention and clarity of intent as part of the evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support must be adequate and intelligible once weight is known
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the moment that the conditions of weight are comprehended, both truth and feeling require that the conditions of support should be also comprehended'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an observer can perceive the load a member must carry, the means of support should be evident and honest. Avoid tricks of support that, when the conditions are clear, are obviously insufficient or merely theatrical. Evaluate supports for visible adequacy, not merely for appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of iron and metals: permissible as cement, not as primary support
rubrics_metrics.description: Metals 'may, and sometimes must, enter into the construction to a certain extent, as nails in wooden architecture ... metals may be used as a cement but not as a support'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat metal elements as acceptable when they perform a cementing, tying, or auxiliary role (rivets, bands that could be superseded by good cement). Consider it a violation of the art where metal takes the place of stone or wood as primary load-bearing element (e.g., cast-iron spires or iron roofs/pillars are 'not architecture' in the author's assumption). Establish a stop-rule: metal may assist but should not supplant the structural role of traditional materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain historical materials/principles to preserve architectural character
rubrics_metrics.description: 'one of the chief dignities of architecture is its historical use; and since the latter is partly dependent on consistency of style, it will be felt right to retain as far as may be, even in periods of more advanced science, the materials and principles of earlier ages'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging innovations (new materials or methods), weigh their impact on historical continuity and stylistic consistency. Prefer retention of earlier materials/principles where they contribute to the identity and dignity of the art, unless a new coherent architectural system is consciously developed for the new materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish imagination from deception — imagination must confess its ideality
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the imagination is a voluntary summoning of the conceptions of things absent or impossible ... it is a noble faculty so long as it confesses its own ideality; when it ceases to confess this, it is insanity'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating representational work, accept imaginative invention that is honest about its nature (not claiming presence or empirical truth). Deceptive assertions of existence or false statements of form/color are lies; imaginative depiction that does not assert physical existence is permissible and noble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitual truthfulness and avoidance of petty untruths
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Do not let us lie at all. Do not think of one falsity as harmless, and another as slight ... Speaking truth is like writing fair, and comes only by practice'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the ethical character of the practitioner: habitual small falsities erode moral and artistic integrity. Encourage forming the habit of truth in both speech and craftsmanship; consider petty, casual untruths as formative of worse deception and harmful to the art's dignity.
